question: ¿Cómo reduce QLoRA la memoria de ajuste del modelo? Cita el artículo.

messages.content: ¿Cómo reduce QLoRA la memoria de ajuste del modelo? Cita el artículo.

response.answer:
## Cómo reduce QLoRA la memoria del ajuste fino

**La idea central.** QLoRA no inventa una técnica única, sino que combina dos movimientos: congela el modelo base y lo cuantiza a 4 bits, y sobre esa base congelada entrena un conjunto pequeño de adaptadores de bajo rango (LoRA) en precisión de 16 bits, retropropagando gradientes **a través** de los pesos cuantizados ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A1)). El resultado declarado es que el ajuste fino de un modelo de 65 000 millones de parámetros pasa de requerir **más de 780 GB** de memoria de GPU a **menos de 48 GB**, sin degradar el tiempo de ejecución ni el rendimiento predictivo respecto a una línea base ajustada por completo en 16 bits ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A1)).

Conviene precisar el matiz: el artículo afirma que demuestra «por primera vez que es posible ajustar un modelo cuantizado a 4 bits sin ninguna degradación de rendimiento» ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A1)), es decir, el ahorro no se paga con calidad.

**Las tres innovaciones.** El resumen del artículo las enumera explícitamente: (a) **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)**, un tipo de dato que se presenta como informacionalmente óptimo para pesos con distribución normal; (b) **Double Quantization**, que reduce la huella media cuantizando las propias constantes de cuantización; y (c) **Paged Optimizers**, para gestionar los picos de memoria ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A0)). El mismo trío se repite en la introducción con una cifra concreta: Double Quantization ahorra del orden de **0,37 bits por parámetro**, aproximadamente **3 GB** en un modelo de 65 000 millones ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A3)).

La sección metodológica describe el mecanismo a dos tipos de dato: QLoRA mantiene un tipo de almacenamiento de baja precisión (habitualmente 4 bits) y un tipo de cómputo (habitualmente BFloat16); cada vez que se usa un tensor de peso QLoRA se **descuantiza a BFloat16** y la multiplicación matricial se hace en 16 bits ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A6)). Ahí está la clave del compromiso: se **almacena** barato, se **calcula** preciso.

Respecto a NF4, el texto lo sitúa sobre la cuantización por cuantiles, un tipo de dato que garantiza que cada *bin* de cuantización reciba el mismo número de valores del tensor de entrada, y señala que su limitación principal es el propio proceso de estimación del cuantil ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A6)).

**Dónde está realmente la memoria.** Este es el punto más interesante y contraintuitivo del artículo. Para un LLaMA de 7 000 millones entrenado con FLAN v2 y tamaño de lote 1, con pesos LoRA equivalentes al 0,2 % habitual de los pesos del modelo, los gradientes de entrada de LoRA ocupan **567 MB**, mientras que los propios parámetros LoRA ocupan solo **26 MB**; con *gradient checkpointing*, los gradientes de entrada bajan a unos 18 MB de media por secuencia, y el modelo base en 4 bits consume **5 048 MB** ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A5)). La conclusión que extraen los autores es doble: el *gradient checkpointing* es importante, y reducir agresivamente la cantidad de parámetros LoRA aporta solo beneficios marginales de memoria — lo que a su vez permite usar más adaptadores sin aumentar significativamente la huella total de entrenamiento ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A5)). En otras palabras: el cuello de botella no son los adaptadores, sino las activaciones y los gradientes, y por eso cuantizar el modelo base es lo que mueve la aguja.

El desglose final de huella lo confirma con cifras por escala (33B: 24,7 GB; 65B: 45,0 GB de referencia) y con los tamaños de Guanaco publicados, desde 5 GB en 7B hasta 41 GB en 65B ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A57)).

**La deuda con LoRA.** QLoRA se apoya en el mecanismo LoRA original, que ya congelaba los pesos preentrenados e inyectaba matrices de descomposición de rango entrenables en cada capa del Transformer, reduciendo los parámetros entrenables **10 000 veces** y el requisito de memoria de GPU **3 veces** frente al ajuste completo de GPT-3 175B con Adam ([Hu et al., 2021](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A5eb237950747b20aa43bb01035bf59bd24bdf57c157b22f45842c261aea271ba%3A0)). Hu et al. cuantifican el beneficio práctico: en GPT-3 175B el consumo de VRAM durante el entrenamiento baja de 1,2 TB a 350 GB, y el tamaño del *checkpoint* se reduce aproximadamente 10 000× (de 350 GB a 35 MB) con r = 4 adaptando solo las proyecciones de *query* y *value* ([Hu et al., 2021](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A5eb237950747b20aa43bb01035bf59bd24bdf57c157b22f45842c261aea271ba%3A11)). El ahorro ahí proviene de no almacenar estados del optimizador para los parámetros congelados ([Hu et al., 2021](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A5eb237950747b20aa43bb01035bf59bd24bdf57c157b22f45842c261aea271ba%3A11)).

**Cómo se articulan ambas contribuciones.** La diferencia es de capa de ataque. LoRA ataca el coste de los **estados del optimizador y de los parámetros entrenables**: congela el modelo y entrena solo adaptadores. QLoRA añade una segunda capa sobre eso, atacando el coste del **modelo base congelado** mediante cuantización a 4 bits, y el coste de los **picos de memoria** mediante *paged optimizers*. La ganancia no es aditiva de forma trivial, porque —como muestra el desglose de memoria— el modelo base en 4 bits (5 048 MB) domina sobre los adaptadores (26 MB) en el caso analizado ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A5)). LoRA reduce lo que se entrena; QLoRA reduce además lo que se almacena.

También hay una diferencia en los resultados comunicados: LoRA motiva su propuesta por la inviabilidad de desplegar instancias independientes de modelos afinados de 175B parámetros ([Hu et al., 2021](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A5eb237950747b20aa43bb01035bf59bd24bdf57c157b22f45842c261aea271ba%3A0)), mientras que QLoRA se presenta como el primer método que ajusta un modelo cuantizado a 4 bits sin degradación y lo demuestra a escala de 65B en una sola GPU ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A1)). El propio QLoRA reconoce su base: en su formalización, la proyección de LoRA se define como Y = XW + s·XL₁L₂, con L₁ y L₂ las matrices de bajo rango y s un escalar ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A5)).

**Síntesis en una frase.** QLoRA reduce memoria en tres frentes simultáneos: cuantiza el modelo base congelado a 4 bits con un tipo de dato diseñado para distribuciones normales (NF4), comprime las constantes de cuantización (Double Quantization, ~0,37 bits/parámetro) y gestiona los picos con paginación del optimizador (Paged Optimizers) — todo ello descuantizando a 16 bits para el cómputo y entrenando solo adaptadores LoRA ([Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A0), [Dettmers et al., 2023](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3Afda6484d8d98842113e597d94278905ab98a6de012c58dcd08a230e6aa97c3a3%3A6)).

---

**Nota sobre la evidencia disponible.** La consulta está cubierta de forma directa y suficiente por el artículo QLoRA, del que se han leído páginas originales, y por el artículo LoRA original, que aporta el mecanismo base. Conviene advertir, no obstante, que buena parte del material recuperado en esta búsqueda corresponde a archivos sintéticos no relacionados con el tema —por ejemplo, notas sobre un sensor de turbidez ([fixture 13](nodus://passage/scoped%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A53d798297a64ddc2de79e78076ac63dc7ed111f8a1b5a92c7ba4c677dd93bd01)), sobre el ensayo Vega de recuperación espaciada ([fixture 07](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A183833a5eb2a4dd9c7e28040f5239e6ca369021c3306a5d232049c2568aa4ca4%3A0)) o sobre la biblioteca de Puerto Claro ([fixture 01](nodus://passage/documentary%3A42aff95b285607f12c25f2a21df75a3a634b1fd8b92dc099fa20a0c656b3c5c1%3A5d812f0a613c9d59b0fd420770fc47dee24666923045812718af63f5e1dcb21e%3A0))— que no sostienen ninguna afirmación sobre QLoRA y que, por tanto, no se citan aquí. La búsqueda en el catálogo por palabras clave de QLoRA no arrojó coincidencias adicionales, y el registro de investigación indica que una búsqueda ulterior solo habría repetido una anterior. No hay contradicciones ni vacíos documentados sobre este punto en el material recuperado.

However, finetuning very large models is prohibitively expensive; regular 16-bit finetuning of a LLaMA 65B parameter model [57] requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory. While recent quantization methods can reduce the memory footprint of LLMs [14, 13, 18, 66], such techniques only work for inference and break down during training [65]. We demonstrate for the first time that it is possible to finetune a quantized 4-bit model without any performance degradation. Our method, QLORA, uses a novel high-precision technique to quantize a pretrained model to 4-bit, then adds a small set of learnable Low-rank Adapter weights [28] ∗Equal contribution. [^2]https://github.com/artidoro/qlora and https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes Preprint. Under review. that are tuned by backpropagating gradients through the quantized weights. QLORA reduces the average memory requirements of finetuning a 65B parameter model from >780GB of GPU memory to <48GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16- bit fully finetuned baseline. This marks a significant largest publicly available models to date finetunable on a single GPU.

# QLORA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs Tim Dettmers∗ Artidoro Pagnoni∗ Ari Holtzman Luke Zettlemoyer University of Washington {dettmers,artidoro,ahai,lsz}@cs.washington.edu ## Abstract We present QLORA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance. QLORA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA). Our best model family, which we name Guanaco, outperforms all previous openly released models on the Vicuna benchmark, reaching 99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT while only requiring 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU. QLORA introduces a number of innovations to save memory without sacrificing performance: (a) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a new data type that is information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights (b) Double Quantization to reduce the average memory footprint by quantizing the quantization constants, and (c) Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes. We use QLORA to finetune more than 1,000 models, providing a detailed analysis of instruction following and chatbot performance across 8 instruction datasets, multiple model types (LLaMA, T5), and model scales that would be infeasible to run with regular finetuning (e.g. 33B and 65B parameter models). Our results show that QLoRA finetuning on a small high-quality dataset leads to state-of-the-art results, even when using smaller models than the previous SoTA. We provide a detailed analysis of chatbot performance based on both human and GPT-4 evaluations showing that GPT-4 evaluations are a cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation. Furthermore, we find that current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy to accurately evaluate the performance levels of chatbots. Edward Hu∗ Yelong Shen∗ Phillip Wallis Zeyuan Allen-Zhu Yuanzhi Li Shean Wang Lu Wang Weizhu Chen yuanzhil, swang, luw, wzchen}@microsoft.com An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pretraining on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. Using GPT-3 175B as an example – deploying independent instances of fine-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively expensive. We propose Low-RankAdaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pretrained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks. Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on-par or better than finetuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite having fewer trainable parameters, a higher training throughput, and, unlike adapters, no additional inference latency. We also provide an empirical investigation into rank-deficiency in language model adaptation, which sheds light on the efficacy of LoRA. We release a package that facilitates the integration of LoRA with PyTorch models and provide our implementations and model checkpoints for RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and GPT-2 at https://github.com/microsoft/LoRA. Many applications in natural language processing rely on adapting one large-scale, pre-trained language model to multiple down-h stream applications. Such adaptation is

a future work. Practical Benefits and Limitations. The most significant benefit comes from the reduction in memory and storage usage. For a large Transformer trained with Adam, we reduce that VRAM usage by up to 2/3 ifr dmodel as we do not need to store the optimizer states for the frozen parameters. On GPT-3 175B, we reduce the VRAM consumption during training from 1.2TB to 350GB. Withr = 4 and only the query and value projection matrices being adapted, the checkpoint size is reduced by roughly 10,000× (from 350GB to 35MB)[^4]. This allows us to train with significantly fewer GPUs and avoid I/O bottlenecks. Another benefit is that we can switch between tasks while deployed at a much lower cost by only swapping the LoRA weights as opposed to all the parameters. This allows for the creation of many customized models that can be swapped in and out on the fly on machines that store the pre-trained weights in VRAM. We also observe a 25% speedup during training on GPT-3 175B compared to full fine-tuning[^5] as we do not need to calculate the gradient for the vast majority of the parameters. LoRA also has its limitations. # QLORA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs Tim Dettmers∗ Artidoro Pagnoni∗ Ari Holtzman Luke Zettlemoyer University of Washington {dettmers,artidoro,ahai,lsz}@cs.washington.edu ## Abstract We present QLORA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance. QLORA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA). Our best model family, which we name Guanaco, outperforms all previous openly released models on the Vicuna benchmark, reaching 99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT while only requiring 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU. QLORA introduces a number of innovations to save memory without sacrificing performance: (a) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a new data type that is information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights (b) Double Quantization to reduce the average memory footprint by quantizing the quantization constants, and (c) Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes. We use QLORA to finetune more than 1,000 models, providing a detailed analysis of instruction following and chatbot performance across 8 instruction datasets, multiple model types (LLaMA, T5), and model scales that would be infeasible to run with regular finetuning (e.g. 33B and 65B parameter models). Our results show that QLoRA finetuning on a small high-quality dataset leads to state-of-the-art results, even when using smaller models than the previous SoTA. We provide a detailed analysis of chatbot performance based on both human and GPT-4 evaluations showing that GPT-4 evaluations are a cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation. Furthermore, we find that current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy to accurately evaluate the performance levels of chatbots. With gradient checkpointing [9], the input gradients reduce to an average of 18 MB per sequence making them more memory intensive than all LoRA weights combined. In comparison, the 4-bit base model consumes 5,048 MB of memory. This highlights that gradient checkpointing is important but also that aggressively reducing the amount of LoRA parameter yields only minor memory benefits. This means we can use more adapters without significantly increasing the overall training memory footprint (see Appendix G for a detailed breakdown). As discussed later, this is crucial for recovering full 16-bit precision performance. ## 3 QLORA Finetuning QLORA achieves high-fidelity 4-bit finetuning via two techniques we propose—4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization and Double Quantization. Additionally, we introduce Paged Optimizers, to prevent memory spikes during gradient checkpointing from causing out-of-memory errors that have traditionally made finetuning on a single machine difficult for large models. QLORA has one low-precision storage data type, in our case usually 4-bit, and one computation data type that is usually BFloat16. In practice, this means whenever a QLORA weight tensor is used, we dequantize the tensor to BFloat16, and then perform a matrix multiplication in 16-bit. Quantile quantization works by estimating the quantile of the input tensor through the empirical cumulative distribution function. Edward Hu∗ Yelong Shen∗ Phillip Wallis Zeyuan Allen-Zhu Yuanzhi Li Shean Wang Lu Wang Weizhu Chen yuanzhil, swang, luw, wzchen}@microsoft.com An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pretraining on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. Using GPT-3 175B as an example – deploying independent instances of fine-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively expensive. We propose Low-RankAdaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pretrained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks. Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on-par or better than finetuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite having fewer trainable parameters, a higher training throughput, and, unlike adapters, no additional inference latency. We also provide an empirical investigation into rank-deficiency in language model adaptation, which sheds light on the efficacy of LoRA. We release a package that facilitates the integration of LoRA with PyTorch models and provide our implementations and model checkpoints for RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and GPT-2 at https://github.com/microsoft/LoRA. For a large Transformer trained with Adam, we reduce that VRAM usage by up to 2/3 ifr dmodel as we do not need to store the optimizer states for the frozen parameters. On GPT-3 175B, we reduce the VRAM consumption during training from 1.2TB to 350GB. Withr = 4 and only the query and value projection matrices being adapted, the checkpoint size is reduced by roughly 10,000× (from 350GB to 35MB)[^4]. This allows us to train with significantly fewer GPUs and avoid I/O bottlenecks. Another benefit is that we can switch between tasks while deployed at a much lower cost by only swapping the LoRA weights as opposed to all the parameters. This allows for the creation of many customized models that can be swapped in and out on the fly on machines that store the pre-trained weights in VRAM. We also observe a 25% speedup during training on GPT-3 175B compared to full fine-tuning[^5] as we do not need to calculate the gradient for the vast majority of the parameters. LoRA also has its limitations. For example, it is not straightforward to batch inputs to different tasks with differentAandBin a single forward pass, if one chooses to absorbAandBintoWto eliminate additional inference latency. Though it is possible to not merge the weights and dynamically choose the LoRA modules to use for samples in a batch for scenarios where latency is not critical. ## 5EMPIRICALEXPERIMENTS We evaluate the downstream task performance of LoRA on RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), De- BERTa (He et al., 2021), and GPT-2 (Radford et al., b),

# QLORA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs Tim Dettmers∗ Artidoro Pagnoni∗ Ari Holtzman Luke Zettlemoyer University of Washington {dettmers,artidoro,ahai,lsz}@cs.washington.edu ## Abstract We present QLORA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance. QLORA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA). Our best model family, which we name Guanaco, outperforms all previous openly released models on the Vicuna benchmark, reaching 99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT while only requiring 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU. QLORA introduces a number of innovations to save memory without sacrificing performance: (a) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a new data type that is information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights (b) Double Quantization to reduce the average memory footprint by quantizing the quantization constants, and (c) Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes. We use QLORA to finetune more than 1,000 models, providing a detailed analysis of instruction following and chatbot performance across 8 instruction datasets, multiple model types (LLaMA, T5), and model scales that would be infeasible to run with regular finetuning (e.g. 33B and 65B parameter models). Our results show that QLoRA finetuning on a small high-quality dataset leads to state-of-the-art results, even when using smaller models than the previous SoTA. We provide a detailed analysis of chatbot performance based on both human and GPT-4 evaluations showing that GPT-4 evaluations are a cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation. Furthermore, we find that current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy to accurately evaluate the performance levels of chatbots. With gradient checkpointing [9], the input gradients reduce to an average of 18 MB per sequence making them more memory intensive than all LoRA weights combined. In comparison, the 4-bit base model consumes 5,048 MB of memory. This highlights that gradient checkpointing is important but also that aggressively reducing the amount of LoRA parameter yields only minor memory benefits. This means we can use more adapters without significantly increasing the overall training memory footprint (see Appendix G for a detailed breakdown). As discussed later, this is crucial for recovering full 16-bit precision performance. ## 3 QLORA Finetuning QLORA achieves high-fidelity 4-bit finetuning via two techniques we propose—4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization and Double Quantization. Additionally, we introduce Paged Optimizers, to prevent memory spikes during gradient checkpointing from causing out-of-memory errors that have traditionally made finetuning on a single machine difficult for large models. QLORA has one low-precision storage data type, in our case usually 4-bit, and one computation data type that is usually BFloat16. In practice, this means whenever a QLORA weight tensor is used, we dequantize the tensor to BFloat16, and then perform a matrix multiplication in 16-bit. We now discuss the components of QLORA followed by a formal definition of QLORA. 4-bit NormalFloat Quantization The NormalFloat (NF) data type builds on Quantile Quantization [15] which is an information-theoretically optimal data type that ensures each quantization bin has an equal number of values assigned from the input tensor. Quantile quantization works by estimating the quantile of the input tensor through the empirical cumulative distribution function.
